unit.title: We need each other more than we think
unit.needIt: Babies need holding as much as feeding, and adults do what the person beside them expects. Knowing how strongly others shape you helps you choose who is beside you.
unit.why: The lecture looks at how humans are built to need others to survive and thrive. It shows that when we feel a real connection, we feel safe, but when that connection is missing, we struggle to trust the world.
unit.outcome: Identify how early bonds and social connections shape your ability to trust and flourish.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you feel a deep bond with a friend or a sense of safety with your family. You also feel it when you struggle to trust a stranger or a new coworker.
unit.do: Reach out to a friend or family member today just to check in and strengthen your social bond.

quiz.q: What was the main goal of the Milgram study?
quiz.why: The study looked at how people follow orders even when they feel bad about it.
quiz.quote: The research that Milgram conducted was inspired by an an attempt to understand what could possibly have explained the behavior of ordinary German citizens in Nazi Germany.

quiz.q: What happened when subjects felt bad about the shocks?
quiz.why: The lecture describes subjects sweating, stuttering, and biting their lips.
quiz.quote: Many subjects showed signs of nervousness, especially upon administering the more powerful shocks in a large number of cases, the degree of tension reached extremes rarely seen in such laboratory subjects.

quiz.q: How did the presence of the experimenter affect obedience?
quiz.why: People were less likely to obey when the person giving orders was not right there.
quiz.quote: And the tendency of subjects to collaborate, to cooperate, to do what was asked of them, declined directly with whether the experimenter was present in the room with them.

quiz.why: The wire mother had milk but the cloth mother provided comfort.
quiz.quote: The wire mother had milk, and they needed to go to her to get food. But the cloth mother had comfort, and if they wanted to be consoled, they needed to go to her.

quiz.q: What is a result of secure attachment?
quiz.why: Secure attachment creates a sense that the world is a safe and cooperative place.
quiz.quote: The world becomes a place in which social trust is possible, and the early instincts that you come to have when presented with the faces and bodies of conspecifics cause you later on to have as your most primitive response pattern an expectation that if there's no evidence to the contrary, that conspecific is going to be to be responsive to your honest and expressed needs.

quiz.q: How does social interaction affect physical health in older adults?
quiz.why: The lecture lists several physical benefits of social interaction, including a stronger immune system.
quiz.quote: Having strong social relationships strengthens the immune system. It extends life more than quitting smoking.

quiz.q: What does Aristotle say about friendship?
quiz.why: Aristotle argues that friendship is the most central thing for flourishing at any age.
quiz.quote: nothing plays a more central role in allowing you to flourish than friendship does.

crystal.key: Human flourishing depends on deep social connections and early trust.

decoys.why: The lecture shows that monkeys chose cloth over wire for comfort.

decoys.text: Obedience is always a good trait.
decoys.why: The lecture shows the heavy psychic cost of obeying immoral orders.

crystal.aha: We are built to thrive through emotional bonds and social trust.
